title: Social News Feed UI
prompt: Design the web client for a social app's home feed: an endless list of posts with text, photos, likes and comments, which must feel smooth on a mid-range phone.

clarify.q: Which devices matter most: mobile web, desktop, or both?
clarify.why: Mobile web on a mid-range Android sets the CPU and memory budget. It decides how hard we virtualise and how small the images must be.

clarify.q: What can a post contain: text, one photo, several photos, video, link previews?
clarify.why: Each media type has its own loading strategy. Video changes memory and autoplay rules. A multi-photo post is a carousel inside a list.

clarify.q: Is the feed ranked or chronological, and do new posts appear while I read?
clarify.why: Ranked feeds need an opaque cursor because the order is not a timestamp. Live inserts need a 'new posts' banner, not silent shifting of content under the user's thumb.

clarify.q: Which interactions are in scope: like, comment, share, hide?
clarify.why: Each write needs an optimistic path and a rollback. The list tells us how big the mutation layer has to be.

clarify.q: Does the feed have to be indexed by search engines, or is it behind login?
clarify.why: Behind login means SSR is only for speed (LCP), not SEO, so we can SSR just the first few posts.

clarify.q: Must the user come back to the exact spot after opening a post and pressing Back?
clarify.why: Yes almost always. That forces us to keep the list data in memory or session storage and to restore scroll by anchor, not by pixel.
Showing the last feed offline needs a service worker or IndexedDB cache. Without it, an error state is fine.

functional: Show the home feed, loading more posts automatically as the user nears the end.
Like and unlike a post with instant feedback; add a comment.
Show a 'New posts' banner when fresh posts exist; tapping it scrolls to the top and inserts them.
Open a post detail view and return to the same scroll position with Back.
Show photos at the right resolution for the screen, with no layout jumps while they load.
nonFunctional: LCP under 2.5 s on slow 4G (150 ms RTT, 1.6 Mbps) on a mid-range phone.
Scrolling at 60 fps: no long task over 50 ms while scrolling; INP under 200 ms for the like button.
CLS under 0.1, including when images and new pages load.
Memory stays flat over a 30-minute session (no unbounded DOM or decoded-image growth).
Feed route JavaScript under 150 KB gzipped.
Usable with a screen reader and keyboard: each post is reachable and announced with its position.
outOfScope: The ranking algorithm and the fan-out backend (the backend news-feed problem).
Video autoplay and ads, beyond leaving room for them in the list.

assumptions: Mobile viewport 390 × 800 CSS px, DPR 3; a post card averages 500 px tall, so ~2 posts per screen
A post card is ~150 DOM nodes
Page size 10 posts; one post is ~2 KB of JSON (author, text, counts, image variants, 2 comment previews)
Feed photo: ~80 KB as WebP/AVIF at 1080 px wide
Slow 4G: 150 ms RTT, 1.6 Mbps ≈ 200 KB/s; feed API takes 100 ms on the server
A heavy session scrolls 300 posts in 30 minutes; a fast flick moves ~1 post per second

steps.label: DOM size without virtualisation
steps.math: 300 posts × 150 nodes = 45 000 nodes. Windowed: 2 visible + 3 overscan each side = 8 posts × 150
steps.result: 45 000 vs ~1 200 nodes: style and layout cost grows with the first, stays flat with the second

steps.label: Decoded image memory
steps.math: 1080 × 1350 px × 4 bytes ≈ 5.8 MB per decoded photo. 300 photos ≈ 1.75 GB; 8 photos ≈ 47 MB
steps.result: Keeping every image alive will get the tab killed on a phone; offscreen images must be released

steps.label: One page of feed JSON
steps.math: 10 × 2 KB = 20 KB raw ≈ 6 KB gzip. 6 KB ÷ 200 KB/s = 30 ms + 150 ms RTT + 100 ms server
steps.result: ≈ 280 ms per page: JSON is cheap

steps.label: One page of photos
steps.result: ≈ 4 s: images are the real cost, so load only those near the viewport (2 per screen ≈ 0.8 s)

steps.label: When to fetch the next page
steps.math: Next page ready ≈ 0.3 s JSON + 0.8 s first two photos ≈ 1.1 s. At 1 post/s the trigger must be > 1.1 posts ahead; add margin
steps.result: Start fetching when 5 posts (~2.5 screens) remain

steps.label: Scroll frame budget
steps.math: 16.7 ms per frame − ~6 ms browser style, layout, paint ≈ 10 ms for JS. Mounting a card ≈ 4 ms on a mid phone
steps.result: At most 2 card mounts per frame; never read layout inside the scroll handler

steps.label: LCP: SSR vs client-only
steps.math: SSR: 3 RTT connect 450 ms + 150 ms request + 200 ms render = 800 ms TTFB; hero photo 80 KB = 400 ms + 150 ms RTT → ≈ 1.35 s. CSR: 800 ms shell + 150 KB JS 750 ms + 500 ms run + 280 ms API + 550 ms photo ≈ 2.9 s
steps.result: SSR the first posts: ≈ 1.4 s vs ≈ 2.9 s (budget 2.5 s)

estimates.takeaway: JSON is cheap: a page is 6 KB. Images and DOM are expensive. Three things follow. Virtualise (or at least skip rendering offscreen posts) to keep the DOM near 1 200 nodes. Load photos only near the viewport, sized with srcset. Server-render the first screen, because client-only rendering misses the 2.5 s LCP budget on slow 4G by about 0.4 s.

api.body: { feedKey: 'home' | 'following', pageSize = 10, prefetchAhead = 5, renderPost?(postId), onImpression?(postId, msVisible) }
api.returns: A role=feed list of PostCard articles, plus loading, end and error rows
api.note: Takes ids, not post objects: each card subscribes to its own post in the store, so a like re-renders one card, not the list.

api.body: { postId, posInSet, setSize: -1 (unknown), onOpen(postId) } ; events: onLike(postId, liked), onComment(postId, text)
api.note: aria-setsize=-1 tells assistive tech the total is unknown in an endless feed.

api.returns: 200 { items: [{ id, authorId, text, media: [{ w, h, blurhash, srcset: [{ url, width }] }], likeCount, likedByMe, commentCount, createdAt }], users: { [id]: { name, avatar } }, nextCursor, hasMore }
api.note: Opaque cursor encodes the ranking position, not an offset. Users come once in a side map so the client can normalise without duplicates.

api.body: Polled every 60 s while the tab is visible
api.note: Returns only a count by default; items fetched when the user taps the banner.
Separate set and unset verbs, not a toggle, so a retried request cannot flip the state twice.
clientId lets the client match the server copy to its optimistic placeholder and lets the server dedupe retries.

entities.name: posts.byId
entities.store: Client normalised store (Redux Toolkit, Zustand or a query cache)
entities.why: One copy of each post. The same post can appear in the home feed, a profile and the detail view; a like updates all of them.

entities.name: users.byId
entities.why: Authors repeat often in a feed. Storing them once saves memory and keeps a name change consistent.

entities.name: feeds[feedKey]
entities.why: The list is just ordered ids plus pagination state. Restoring it from sessionStorage makes Back instant.

entities.name: mutations.byKey
entities.why: Holds what to roll back to and lets rapid taps collapse into one request.

data.note: Cache key for the list is ['feed', feedKey]. URL state is small: /home for the feed and /p/:id for a post. The detail view opens as a route-driven overlay over the still-mounted feed, so the feed keeps its scroll and memory. The scroll anchor (top visible post id plus pixel offset) goes into history.state for a full reload. To cap memory, evict posts from the store that are more than 200 positions away from the viewport and no longer referenced.

hld.summary:
The server streams HTML for the app shell and the first three posts, with the first photo marked fetchpriority=high. The client hydrates and takes over. Feed data enters through one query layer that normalises responses into posts and users and appends ids to feeds.home.ids, de-duplicating by id.

The virtual list renders only posts near the viewport. It measures real heights with ResizeObserver and keeps a sentinel element 5 posts before the end. When the sentinel becomes visible (IntersectionObserver), it asks for the next page. Each PostCard subscribes to its own post id. The mutation layer applies likes to the store at once, sends idempotent requests, and rolls back on failure. A visibility-aware poller fills the 'New posts' banner.

diagram.title: Component tree and data flow
diagram.src:
flowchart TD
  SSR["Streaming SSR (shell + 3 posts)"] --> APP[FeedPage]
  APP --> BANNER[NewPostsBanner]
  APP --> VL["VirtualList (role feed)"]
  VL --> CARD["PostCard (article)"]
  VL --> SENT[Sentinel 5 posts before end]
  CARD --> MEDIA["PostMedia (srcset, aspect-ratio)"]
  CARD --> ACT[ActionBar like and comment]
  SENT -->|visible| Q[Feed query layer]
  Q -->|"GET /v1/feed?cursor"| API[Feed API]
  Q -->|normalise| STORE["Store: posts, users, feeds"]
  STORE --> CARD
  ACT --> MUT[Mutation layer]
  MUT -->|optimistic patch| STORE
  MUT -->|"PUT or DELETE like"| API

flows.title: First load
steps: Server streams the shell, then the first 3 posts as HTML with serialised store data.
First photo has fetchpriority=high and explicit width and height; the rest are loading=lazy.
Client hydrates the cards it was sent; the feed query starts from the server's nextCursor, not from scratch.
The virtual list measures the first cards and starts tracking the sentinel.

flows.title: Scrolling to the next page
steps: Sentinel 5 posts before the end becomes visible.
Query layer checks status is not already 'loading' (no duplicate page requests) and fetches with nextCursor.
Response is normalised; new ids are appended, skipping any id already present.
List adds the new posts; offscreen ones get estimated heights until measured.
Cards far above the viewport unmount; their measured heights stay cached so the scrollbar doesn't jump.

flows.title: Opening a post and coming back
steps: Tap pushes /p/:id; the detail overlay renders from posts.byId at once, then refreshes in the background.
The feed stays mounted underneath, so nothing is refetched.
Back closes the overlay; focus returns to the card that opened it.

deepDives.title: Rendering strategy
deepDives.problem: The feed is personal and behind login, so SEO doesn't matter, but LCP does. A client-only app spends about 2.9 s on slow 4G before the first photo shows. Rendering all of it on the server makes the HTML big and hydration slow.

options.name: Client-side only (CSR)
options.how: Static shell from a CDN; JavaScript fetches the feed and renders.
pros: Simplest to host; shell is cacheable
No server render cost
cons: LCP ≈ 2.9 s on slow 4G, over budget
Blank screen while JavaScript loads

options.name: SSR the first page, then CSR
options.how: Server renders the first 3 posts with their data; client hydrates and paginates.
pros: LCP ≈ 1.4 s: the hero photo is in the HTML
Back/refresh can show content quickly
cons: Server render on every visit (personalised, not cacheable)
Hydration cost on a slow phone

options.name: Streaming SSR with Suspense or server components
options.how: Send the shell at once, stream post HTML as data arrives; non-interactive parts need no hydration.
pros: Earliest first paint; less JavaScript to hydrate
Slow feed queries don't block the shell
cons: Needs a framework that supports it well
Harder to debug; caching rules are subtler

deepDives.choice: Streaming SSR for the shell and first 3 posts, client rendering after that. Only the action bar and media need to be interactive, so keep the hydration surface small. If the team's stack had no streaming support, plain SSR of the first page still meets the budget. If this were a public, cacheable feed, I would cache the rendered page at the CDN.

deepDives.title: Virtualisation and its accessibility cost
deepDives.problem: After 300 posts a plain list holds 45 000 nodes and gigabytes of possible decoded images. Virtualisation fixes that, but it removes content from the DOM. Find-in-page can't find it, screen readers can't reach it, and a focused button that scrolls away gets unmounted, so focus drops to the body.

options.name: Full windowing
options.how: Render only posts in the viewport plus overscan; absolutely position them using measured or estimated heights.
pros: Flat DOM and memory however long the session
Predictable scroll performance
cons: Ctrl+F and screen-reader browse mode can't see unmounted posts
Variable heights need measuring and scroll correction

options.name: content-visibility: auto
options.how: Keep every post in the DOM, but add content-visibility: auto and contain-intrinsic-size: auto 500px so the browser skips layout and paint offscreen.
pros: Find-in-page and accessibility tree keep working
Just CSS, no scroll math
cons: DOM nodes and JS objects still grow
Doesn't free image memory by itself

options.name: Hybrid
options.how: content-visibility for the first ~100 posts; beyond that, window out posts far from the viewport and replace them with sized spacers.
pros: Normal sessions get full accessibility
Very long sessions still stay bounded
cons: Two code paths
Behaviour changes partway through a session

deepDives.choice: Hybrid, with these rules for the windowed part: wrap posts in role=feed, each card an article with aria-posinset and aria-setsize=-1; set aria-busy on the feed while appending. Never unmount the card that holds focus. Support Page Down / Page Up between articles. Use overflow-anchor or manual anchoring so measuring a card above the viewport doesn't shift what the user is reading. If the product had short feeds (under 100 posts), content-visibility alone is enough.

deepDives.title: Pagination and new posts
deepDives.problem: A ranked feed changes while you read it. With offset paging, new posts at the top push everything down, so page 2 repeats posts from page 1, or skips some. New content must not jump the list under the user's thumb.

options.name: Offset and limit
options.how: Client asks for ?offset=20&limit=10; server skips the first 20 ranked rows.
pros: Trivial; can jump to page N
cons: Duplicates and gaps when items are inserted
Deep offsets are slow on the server

options.name: Opaque cursor
options.how: Server returns nextCursor encoding the last ranking position (score plus id, or a snapshot id). Client passes it back unchanged.
pros: Stable under inserts
Server can change the encoding freely
cons: No jump to page N
Cursors may expire; client must handle 410 by restarting

options.name: Snapshot the ranked list
options.how: Server ranks once per session and stores the id list; pages are slices of that snapshot.
pros: Perfectly stable order for the session
cons: Server storage per session
Fresh posts only appear through the banner

deepDives.choice: Opaque cursor, with client-side de-duplication by id as a safety net. New posts never insert themselves: a poller every 60 s (paused when document.hidden) fills a 'New posts' banner, and the user chooses to load them. On a 410 'cursor expired', keep what is shown and restart from the top behind the banner. A snapshot is worth it if the ranking is expensive and must be stable across devices.

deepDives.title: Optimistic likes with rollback
deepDives.problem: The like must flip instantly (INP under 200 ms), but the request can take 300 ms or fail. Users double-tap, tap like then unlike quickly, or lose signal. A naive toggle endpoint retried after a timeout can flip the like twice.

options.name: Pessimistic
options.how: Disable the button, wait for the server, then update.
pros: Never shows a wrong state
cons: 300+ ms of lag on every tap; feels broken on slow 4G

options.name: Optimistic with snapshot rollback
options.how: Save the previous value, patch the store, send the request; on error restore the snapshot and show a toast.
pros: Instant feedback
Simple
cons: Rapid taps race: an older failure can roll back a newer success

options.name: Optimistic with intent coalescing
options.how: Store desired and confirmed values per post. Each tap changes desired. One request at a time sends the latest desired value with PUT or DELETE. On success set confirmed; if desired still differs, send again. On error set desired back to confirmed.
pros: Any number of taps gives at most 2 requests
Idempotent verbs make retries safe
No race between old and new responses
cons: More state to hold and test

deepDives.choice: Intent coalescing with PUT/DELETE. The count shown is derived: server count adjusted by (desired − confirmed). Retry network errors twice with backoff before rolling back. On a 404 (post deleted) remove the card. Comments use the same idea with a clientId: show a 'sending' comment at once, and replace it when the server copy arrives with the same clientId.

diagram.title: Like with coalescing and rollback
diagram.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant S as Store
  participant M as Mutation layer
  participant A as API
  U->>S: tap like, desired true
  S-->>U: heart filled, count plus 1
  M->>A: PUT like
  U->>S: tap again, desired false
  A-->>M: 200 liked true
  M->>M: confirmed true, desired differs
  M->>A: DELETE like
  A-->>M: 503 after 2 retries
  M->>S: desired back to confirmed true
  S-->>U: heart filled, toast Could not unlike

deepDives.title: Image loading without layout shift
deepDives.problem: Photos are 90% of the bytes. Load them all and a page costs 4 s on slow 4G. Load them late and users scroll into grey boxes. Load them without known sizes and every photo pushes the text below it, which breaks CLS and the virtual list's height math.

options.name: Native lazy loading plus srcset
options.how: img with srcset (360w, 720w, 1080w), sizes='100vw', loading=lazy, decoding=async, width and height from the API.
pros: No JavaScript; the browser picks the size for DPR and width
Width and height give the box its aspect ratio before load
cons: The browser's lazy-load distance isn't tunable
No control over priority among many images

options.name: IntersectionObserver with a custom margin
options.how: Set src when the image is within 1.5 screens, using a rootMargin; release it when far away.
pros: Tunable look-ahead
Can drop src far offscreen to free decoded memory
cons: More code; must not break no-JS SSR markup

options.name: Placeholder strategy
options.how: Reserve the box with aspect-ratio; show a dominant colour or tiny blurhash until the photo decodes.
pros: Zero CLS
Feels faster than grey boxes
cons: Blurhash decode costs CPU per image
A few hundred bytes more JSON per post

deepDives.choice: All three in layers. The API sends width and height, and CSS aspect-ratio reserves the box, so CLS is zero and the virtual list knows the height before the image loads. Native loading=lazy with srcset for normal posts; the first photo is eager with fetchpriority=high. Windowing releases offscreen images. A dominant-colour placeholder is cheaper than blurhash on low-end phones. Serve AVIF with a WebP fallback from an image CDN. On a Save-Data connection, cap the srcset at 720w.

failures: Keep shown posts; replace the sentinel with an inline 'Couldn't load more · Retry' row; auto-retry once with backoff when the tab is visible and online.
Roll desired back to confirmed, show a short toast, keep the button enabled.
Same post arrives on two pages
De-duplicate by id when appending; the normalised store already holds one copy.
Memory grows over a long session
Window out far posts, release offscreen image src, evict store entries more than 200 positions away.
Back button lands at the top
Keep the feed mounted under the overlay; on reload restore from the sessionStorage list and the anchor (post id + offset) in history.state.
Post text contains HTML or a malicious link
Render text as text nodes; linkify with a parser that builds anchor elements; set rel=noopener ugc on external links; strict CSP.
scale: Heavier posts (video, carousels): one active video at a time, chosen by IntersectionObserver ratio; poster frames reserve the box; pause and release offscreen players.
Lower-end devices: smaller pages (5), more aggressive windowing, no blurhash, and reduce overscan to 1 post each side.
More surfaces reusing posts (profile, search, groups): the normalised store pays off: every list is just ids, and a like shows everywhere at once.

followups.q: How do you measure scroll smoothness in the field?
answer: Long Animation Frames API to catch frames over 50 ms during scroll, sampled from real users.
INP for taps on like and comment, split by device class.
Track blank-area time: how often the user sees a placeholder instead of a post.

followups.q: Why not just a 'Load more' button?
answer: It is the most accessible choice: content stays in the DOM, footer is reachable, users keep control.
It costs engagement on mobile, which is why product teams usually pick infinite scroll.
A good compromise: auto-load the first few pages, then show a button.

followups.q: What about keyboard users in an endless feed?
answer: Use role=feed: Page Down/Up move between articles; provide a 'skip to end of feed' link.
Each article has a label (author and time) and a reachable action bar.
Don't trap the footer: offer the button after N pages or a fixed footer link.

followups.q: How would you add real-time like counts?
answer: Only for posts in the viewport: subscribe ids over one WebSocket or SSE channel, unsubscribe when they leave.
Batch updates per animation frame so 50 posts updating don't cause 50 renders.
Never overwrite an in-flight optimistic value: merge server counts with desired minus confirmed.

followups.q: How do you make Back restore position after a full reload?
answer: Save the ids and cursor to sessionStorage on pagehide.
Save an anchor (top post id plus offset) in history.state, not a pixel scroll value, because heights are estimates.
On load, render the list, scroll the anchor post into view, then apply the offset.

mistakes: Using offset pagination for a ranked, live feed, then fighting duplicates.
Virtualising without saying what it does to find-in-page, screen readers and focus.
Images without width and height, so every photo load shifts the page and breaks the height estimates.
Storing posts nested inside each feed, so one like needs updating in three places.
A toggle like endpoint, which double-flips when a request is retried.

mid: Defined the feed API with a cursor and explained why not offset
Used IntersectionObserver with a sentinel to trigger the next page, and guarded against duplicate requests
Made the like optimistic and rolled it back on error
Set width and height or aspect-ratio on images and used loading=lazy
Handled loading, end-of-feed and error rows
senior: Did the DOM and image-memory arithmetic and used it to justify virtualisation
Named the accessibility costs of virtualisation and proposed role=feed, aria-posinset, keeping the focused card mounted
Normalised posts and users, with the feed as a list of ids
Chose SSR or streaming for the first screen based on the LCP numbers
Coalesced rapid like taps and used idempotent PUT/DELETE
Restored scroll by anchor, not by pixel
staff: Proposed field metrics: LCP, INP, long animation frames, blank-area time, by device class
Planned memory eviction for long sessions (store and decoded images)
Discussed the hybrid content-visibility plus windowing approach and when to switch
Covered image CDN, AVIF/WebP, Save-Data, and one-video-at-a-time policy
